SOP → circuit: the recipe

blocks.caption:
Inverters make the barred
letters, each AND gate makes one minterm, and one OR gate joins
them.

blocks.html:
1. Put a NOT gate on any input that appears with a bar.
  2. Make one AND gate per product term.
  3. Feed all AND outputs into one OR gate.
blocks.text:
Put a NOT gate on any input that appears with a
bar. Make one AND gate per product term. Feed all AND outputs into one OR gate .

blocks.html: This is called two-level logic (level 1: AND, level 2: OR; the NOT gates don’t count as a level).
blocks.text:
This is called two-level logic (level 1: AND, level
2: OR; the NOT gates don’t count as a level).

blocks.html: Example: Y = A̅B̅C̅ + AB̅C̅ + AB̅C needs 3 NOT gates, 3 three-input AND gates and 1 three-input OR gate.

The POS recipe

blocks.html:
1. Find the rows where F = 0.
  2. Write the maxterm for each.
  3. AND them all together.

sections.title: Universal Gates — Building Everything from NAND or NOR

blocks.html: Start here Imagine a LEGO box with only one kind of brick, yet you can still build anything. NAND gates are like that: with enough NAND gates, you can build NOT, AND, OR and every other circuit. Chip factories love this, because making one kind of gate again and again is cheap and fast.
blocks.text:
Start here Imagine a LEGO box with only one kind of brick, yet you can still build anything.
NAND gates are like that: with enough NAND gates, you can build NOT,
AND, OR and every other circuit. Chip factories love this, because
making one kind of gate again and again is cheap and fast.

blocks.caption:
Only NAND bricks: 1 brick makes
NOT, 2 make AND, 3 make OR.

blocks.text: What “universal” means

blocks.html: A gate is universal if NOT, AND and OR (and so any circuit) can be built from it alone. NAND and NOR are both universal.
blocks.text: A gate is universal if NOT, AND and OR (and so any circuit) can be built from it alone. NAND and NOR are both universal.

Two-level circuits:
AND-OR becomes NAND-NAND

blocks.caption:
Replace every gate in an AND-OR circuit
with a NAND. The output stays exactly the same.

blocks.html: Rule 1: an AND–OR (SOP) circuit = a NAND–NAND circuit with the same shape. Just swap every gate for a NAND.
blocks.text:
Rule 1: an AND–OR (SOP) circuit = a NAND–NAND circuit with the same shape .
Just swap every gate for a NAND.

blocks.html: Why? Put two “bubbles” (NOTs) on each wire between the levels. Two NOTs cancel, so nothing changes. Then the AND + bubble becomes NAND, and the bubbles + OR becomes NAND too (De Morgan).
blocks.text:
Why? Put two “bubbles” (NOTs) on each wire between
the levels. Two NOTs cancel, so nothing changes. Then the AND + bubble
becomes NAND, and the bubbles + OR becomes NAND too (De Morgan).

blocks.html: Rule 2: an OR–AND (POS) circuit = a NOR–NOR circuit with the same shape.
blocks.text: Rule 2: an OR–AND (POS) circuit = a NOR–NOR circuit with the same shape.

blocks.html:
Watch out for single letters. If a product term is just one letter (like A in A + BC), it needs a NAND used as an inverter in the NAND–NAND version.

Example: A + BC → G1 = NAND(A, A) = A̅; G2 = NAND(B, C); out = NAND(G1, G2) → 3 NAND gates.

blocks.text: Multilevel logic

blocks.html: So far we’ve built two-level circuits (AND then OR). Real circuits often use more levels, because that can save gates.
blocks.text:
So far we’ve built two-level circuits (AND then OR).
Real circuits often use more levels , because that can
save gates.

blocks.caption:
Y = (A + B)(C̅ + D) + E̅ uses three
levels of gates, but fewer gates than its two-level version.

blocks.html: Example: Y = (A + B)·(C̅ + D) + E̅
blocks.text: Example: Y = (A + B)·(C̅ + D) + E̅

blocks.html:
• Multilevel: 2 ORs → 1 AND → 1 OR (plus inverters).
  • Two-level SOP: multiply out → AC̅ + AD + BC̅ + BD + E̅. That’s 4 ANDs + one big 5-input OR. More gates.
blocks.text:
Multilevel: 2 ORs → 1 AND → 1 OR (plus
inverters). Two-level SOP: multiply out → AC̅ + AD + BC̅ + BD +
E̅. That’s 4 ANDs + one big 5-input OR. More gates.

blocks.html: Trade-off: multilevel = fewer gates (cheaper) but more levels = slower (the signal passes through more gates).
blocks.text:
Trade-off: multilevel = fewer gates
(cheaper) but more levels = slower (the signal
passes through more gates).

blocks.caption:
Five cooks working at once finish fast.
Three cooks passing one plate along need fewer people but take longer.
Gates work the same way.

blocks.text: Timing diagrams

blocks.html: A timing diagram shows how signals change over time. Each signal is a line that is high (1) or low (0).
blocks.text:
A timing diagram shows how signals change over time . Each signal is a line that is high
(1) or low (0) .

blocks.caption:
Cut the diagram into time slices.
Each slice gives one row of the truth table.

blocks.text:
How to turn a
timing diagram into a function

blocks.html:
1. Draw vertical lines wherever any input changes. This cuts time into slices.
  2. In each slice, read every input (0 or 1) and the output.
  3. Write each slice as a row of a truth table.
  4. Rows that never appear are “don’t care” (you can choose 0 or 1, whichever makes the circuit smaller).
  5. Simplify to get the function.

blocks.html: Why these numbers (Level 1 → 3):
blocks.text: Why these numbers (Level 1 → 3):

blocks.html:
• NOT from NAND: tie both inputs together. NAND(A, A) = NOT(A·A) = NOT A → 1 gate.
  • AND from NAND: NAND gives NOT(AB). Flip it with one more NAND → 2 gates.
  • OR from NAND: De Morgan says A + B = NOT(Ā·B̄) = NAND(Ā, B̄). Making Ā and B̄ costs 2 → total 3.
  • NOR is the mirror image: OR = 2, AND = 3.

blocks.html: How to solve:
blocks.text: How to solve:

blocks.html:
1. Spot the shortcut: X̄ + Ȳ = NAND(X, Y) → G1, 1 gate, no NOTs needed.

  3. SOP → NAND–NAND: G2 = NAND(G1, Z), G3 = NAND(G1, W), F = NAND(G2, G3)
  4. Count: G1, G2, G3, F = 4 ✔ (a computer search confirmed 3 is impossible)

blocks.text: The whole week in 8 lines

blocks.html:
1. SOP → circuit: NOTs → one AND per term → one OR. This is two-level logic.
  2. Canonical ≠ minimal. Σm(3,4,5,6,7) = A + BC.
  3. POS uses the 0-rows. Each gives a maxterm: 0 → A, 1 → A̅, joined by OR. Then AND them all.
  4. Σ ↔︎ Π → use the missing numbers. F ↔︎ F̅ → also the missing numbers. Both → the same numbers.
  5. NAND and NOR are universal. Each one alone can build anything.
  6. Gate counts: NAND: NOT 1, AND 2, OR 3, XOR 4, XNOR 5. NOR: NOT 1, OR 2, AND 3, XNOR 4, XOR 5.
  7. AND–OR = NAND–NAND, and OR–AND = NOR–NOR (same shape, swap the gates).
  8. Timing diagram: slice wherever an input changes → truth table → simplify. “Any one flip changes the output” = XOR.

Common mistakes

blocks.html:
Mistake Correct way
Using the SOP literal rule for maxterms Maxterm: 0 → A, 1 → A̅
Treating a NOT as free in a NAND-only circuit Every NOT costs 1 NAND
